claims.claim: The page explains what the Senate filibuster is and how it works
claims.sourceSpan: a loosely defined term for action designed to prolong debate and delay or prevent a vote on a bill, resolution, amendment, or other debatable question

claims.claim: A filibuster is any tactic that blocks a Senate measure by keeping it from a vote
claims.sourceSpan: includes any use of dilatory or obstructive tactics to block a measure by preventing it from coming to a vote

claims.claim: Cloture under Rule XXII is the only rule that ends debate
claims.sourceSpan: The only Senate rule that permits the body, by vote, to bring consideration of a matter to an end is paragraph 2 of Rule XXII, known as the cloture rule

claims.claim: Cloture has three different thresholds
claims.sourceSpan: The majority required to invoke cloture for most business is three-fifths of the Senators duly chosen and sworn, or 60 votes if there are no vacancies in the Senate's membership. However, invoking cloture on a measure or motion to amend the Senate's standing rules requires the votes of two-thirds of the Senators present and voting, or 67 votes if all 100 Senators vote. Additionally, under precedents established on November 21, 2013, and April 6, 2017, invoking cloture on presidential nominations requires a vote of a majority of Senators present and voting, or 51 votes if all 100 Senators vote

claims.sourceSpan: The only Senate rule that permits the body, by vote, to bring consideration of a matter to an end is paragraph 2 of Rule XXII, known as the cloture rule

claims.claim: REMOVED, the batch shared defect (cross-cutting sweep finding, independently re-confirmed here): "In 2013, the Senate Democratic majority invoked the nuclear option - changing Senate rules by simple majority vote - to eliminate the filibuster for executive branch nominations and lower federal court nominations. In 2017, the Senate Republican majority extended the elimination to Supreme Court nominations." Rule XXII paragraph 2 requires two-thirds of Senators present and voting to invoke cloture on a measure to amend the standing rules, and in the CURRENT Senate Manual (S. Doc. 118-1) that paragraph still carries exactly one amendment footnote, S. Res. 28 of Feb. 27, 1986. The Senate Historical Office calls the 2010s actions "new precedents"; CRS R44819 describes both as reinterpretations effected by a majority overturning a ruling of the chair. Replaced with the dated CRS account and the Senate’s own wording. The identical sentence in cloture-60-vote.html is fixed in the same batch.

REMOVED, F-FAIL: "60 senators out of 100, or a simple majority of those present and voting if there are vacancies." Wrong twice over. Three-fifths of Senators duly chosen and sworn already self-adjusts for vacancies, and no cloture threshold is a simple majority of those present and voting - the present-and-voting measure belongs to the two-thirds threshold for amending the standing rules, which the article never mentioned at all. Replaced with CRS 98-425 stating all three thresholds.

REMOVED, F-FAIL: "All executive branch and judicial nominations now require only a simple majority (51 votes, or 50 plus the Vice President’s tiebreaker)." This conflates the cloture threshold with the confirmation vote, and 51 is not what the precedents set: CRS states the requirement as a majority of Senators PRESENT AND VOTING, which is 51 only if all 100 vote. Replaced with the CRS wording plus CRS’s own caution that the cloture step itself was not removed.

REMOVED, imprecise: "After filing, there’s a mandatory two-day wait before the cloture vote." Rule XXII lays the motion before the Senate "one hour after the Senate meets on the following calendar day but one" - a session-day formula, not a two-day clock. Replaced with the rule’s words and CRS 98-425’s Monday-to-Wednesday worked example.

REMOVED, unsourced: "The process is limited by the Byrd Rule and can only be used once per budget resolution." Nothing in 2 U.S.C. 641 or 644 states a once-per-resolution limit; 641(a) contemplates directives on spending, revenues, the debt limit, or any combination of them. Replaced with the Byrd rule as the statute states it, plus the 641(g) Social Security bar.

REMOVED, unsourced: "Reconciliation requires only 51 votes", and "it has been the vehicle for major tax and spending legislation from both parties." Replaced with the actual mechanism - 2 U.S.C. 641(e)(2)’s 20-hour statutory debate cap - which is the same construction the audited congressional-review-act explainer already uses for 5 U.S.C. 802(d)(2).

REMOVED, wrong mechanism: "When you see a bill stuck at a Senate committee stage for months despite strong House passage and public support, the filibuster is often why." Filibusters and cloture operate on matters pending before the Senate, not in committee, and CRS warns directly against inferring a filibuster from circumstance. Replaced with CRS’s sourced account of floor-time scarcity and pre-emptive accommodation.

REMOVED, unsourced and contradicted by the site’s own pages: "A measure that does pass the Senate has generally either achieved 60-vote support, was processed through a procedure that bypasses the filibuster (reconciliation), or was subject to one of the specific carve-outs the Senate has adopted over the years." The site’s own unanimous-consent explainer and its corpus record show measures passing with no cloture vote at all - 119-S-1884 passed the Senate by unanimous consent on 2025-12-10.

REMOVED, naming and mechanism error: "Certain resolutions under the War Powers Resolution Act receive expedited consideration that limits debate." The statute is the War Powers Resolution, not the War Powers Resolution Act, and 50 U.S.C. 1546 sets reporting and voting DEADLINES rather than a debate cap. Replaced with what 1546 and 1546a actually provide. 1546a’s general procedure incorporates section 601(b) of a 1976 Act which the Code itself notes "was not classified to the Code" and is therefore not fetchable - no claim rests on it.

REMOVED, unsourced editorialising: "one of the most consequential features of the U.S. legislative process"; "In practice, the filibuster is now mostly invisible"; "Since most legislation can’t get 60 Senate votes, the filibuster is effectively a 60-vote threshold for most bills"; "Senators vote for cloture and against the underlying bill regularly"; "The structural choice of process tells you something about the political environment the bill operates in." Each was replaced by a sourced statement or dropped.
REMOVED from Key Sources and the JSON-LD citation array: the Senate cloture-counts table, which this page no longer draws on. It stays live and is cited by cloture-60-vote.html, which does use it.

CROSS-PAGE CONSISTENCY FIX, found in the main thread by reading the freshly audited appropriations-process explainer rather than by any verifier. Both this page and its sibling said, in effect, that vacancies lower the cloture number. That is wrong for the FIRST vacancy: three-fifths of 99 is 59.4, which rounds up to 60. CRS R47106 - already stored, and the source the audited appropriations-process page quotes for exactly this threshold - states it precisely as "a vote of three-fifths of all Senators (60 votes if there is no more than one vacancy)". Both pages now carry that formulation, so all three audited pages agree.

MAIN-THREAD FRESH READ (mine, not an agent's) after round 3, straight through as a reader. Three fixes, one of them a real error no verifier caught. (1) ERROR: the page said 50 U.S.C. 1546a "limits debate on a veto message for one of these measures", where "these measures" meant the CONCURRENT resolutions of 50 U.S.C. 1546. A concurrent resolution is never presented to the President and cannot be vetoed. 1546a in fact governs "Any joint resolution or bill introduced in either House which requires the removal of United States Armed Forces engaged in hostilities" - a different vehicle - and the page now says so. (2) "Passing a bill takes a majority; ending debate on it can take 60" was my own unsourced framing; replaced with CRS RL30360 stating both halves itself. (3) "The threshold has moved once since" was ambiguous next to a later section about the nominations threshold moving; now reads "The threshold for legislation has moved once since."
